newsitem.title: USA: Hollywood, Broadway join to raise Democratic funds.
newsitem.headline: Hollywood, Broadway join to raise Democratic funds.

text.p: Hollywood and Broadway combined on Monday to help President Clinton and Vice President Al Gore raise about $2.7 million for the debt-ridden Democratic Party.

Clinton and Gore were the guests of honour at a fund-raising performance at St. James Theatre of a Broadway show, "A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum." The slapstick musical features Whoopi Goldberg, who played to Clinton throughout, teasing him for his tardiness and blowing kisses to him at the close.

The musical is set in ancient Rome among eunuchs, courtesans, aristocrats and slaves. In a playful mood after the show, Clinton joined the cast on stage and persuaded the three eunuchs to perform the Macarena dance behind Gore, who burst out laughing when he turned around.

"Someone told me that the last time anything like this was done on Broadway was for President (Dwight) Eisenhower in 1955. All I can say is, the others don't know what they missed," Clinton said after the performance.

Hollywood stars Lauren Bacall, Glen Close, Andy Garcia and Andie MacDowell, as well as Goldberg, supermodel Christie Brinkley and jazz artist Wynton Marsalis, were among the celebrities at a money-raising dinner afterward at the Plaza Hotel in Manhattan. Actress Julia Roberts had been expected, but was not seen at the dinner.
"Have you ever in your life been to a Democratic Party event that you've enjoyed more than this evening," Gore told the dinner guests.

In Boston earlier in the day, Clinton laughed it up and posed for pictures with comedian Chevy Chase at a fund-raising lunch that also featured Massachusetts Democratic Sens. Ted Kennedy and John Kerrey.

In remarks to 500 people at the lunch, half of whom were invited as thanks for past work and were not asked to give money, Clinton said he appreciated Boston's support in the year after Republicans took control of Congress in 1994 elections and his own re-election in 1996 looked doubtful.

"Thank you for being here for us in 1995, when everyone said the days of our administration were numbered, the Democratic Party was on a downhill. You know all that stuff they said. You were right, and they were wrong, and I thank you for that," Clinton said to applause in a crowded ballroom at the Copley Plaza Hotel.

Democratic National Committee officials said the party's debt hanging over from last year's campaigns totalled $14.4 million but only 15 cents out of every dollar raised was going to debt reduction. The rest was being spent on organising campaigns, helping candidates and building up the party, they said.

The Boston fund-raiser accepted contributions of $500 to $25,000. In New York a reception cost $1,000 per person, dinner was $5,000 a plate, and the Broadway show required donations of $125 to $25,000. Officials said about $1.2 million was raised in Boston and $1.5 million in New York.

After controversy over the way Democrats raised money last year, which has led to a Justice Department investigation and Senate oversight hearings that start next week, Clinton proposed to reform the way campaigns are financed to ban large, unregulated "soft money" contributions.

In the last few months, he has alternated between urging Congress to reform campaign financing and encouraging big-money contributors to dig deep into their pockets for the soft money contributions that would be banned under reform.
Just last Saturday, Clinton lamented the fact that Congress would not approve campaign finance reform by the July 4 deadline he proposed in his State of the Union address in January.
